The abstract of the article *Studies of interference in serial verbal reactions* in the Journal of Experimental Psychology^[[https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1936-01863-001](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1936-01863-001)] reads:

> In this study pairs of conflicting stimuli, both being inherent aspects of the same symbols, were presented simultaneously (a name of one color printed in the ink of another color—a word stimulus and a color stimulus). The difference in time for reading the words printed in colors and the same words printed in black is the measure of interference of color stimuli upon reading words. The interference of conflicting color stimuli upon the time for reading 100 words (each word naming a color unlike the ink-color of its print) caused an increase of 2.3 seconds or 5.6% over the normal time for reading the same words printed in black.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" version='instructions'}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](https://github.com/earobinson95/stat323-calpoly/blob/main/flipped-style/06-random-and-mixed/images/black-diffcol-texts.png?raw=true){fig-align='center' width=60%}
:::
:::


The article reports on the results of a study in which seventy college undergraduates were given forms with 100 names of colors written in black ink, and the same 100 names of colors written in another color (i.e., the word purple written in green ink). The total time (in seconds) for
reading the 100 words printed in black, and the total time (in seconds) for reading the 100 words printed in different colors were recorded for each subject. The order in which the forms (black or color) were given was randomized to the subjects.

## Part B: Paired t-test

### 3.	Using the skills from your Stat I/II course, conduct and interpret a paired t-test. 

:::callout-note
# Paired t-test in R

Most of you probably have not conducted this analysis in R! There are two ways to do it, which will get you the same answer! 

You will want to use **wide** data for this.

1. `pair_test <- t.test(wide_data$dif_var)`
2. `pair_test <- t.test(wide_data$resp1, wide_data$resp2, paired = T)`

(You should be able to figure out why both work based on your previous stat classes.)

To get the standard error estimate:

### 5. Why is it important the researchers randomized the order in which the forms (black or different color) were given to subjects?

:::{.version-solution}

*This is still implementing random assignment between our experimental units within each block. If we didn't randomize the order, then effects could be confounded by the order.*
:::

### 6. Define the statistical effects model in context.

Based on your treatment and design structure above, fill in the below to define the parameters and random variables given in the statistical effects model in the context of this study. Also indicate what values the indices can take.

$$y_{im} = \mu + \tau_i + p_m + \epsilon_{im} \text{ where }  p_m \overset{iid}{\sim}  N(0,\sigma_{blk}^2) \text{ and }  \epsilon_{im} \overset{iid}{\sim}  N(0,\sigma_\epsilon^2)$$
:::{.version-student .version-instructions}
for $i=$________________;	$m=$________________

where:

+ $y_{ij}$ is the...

+ $\mu$ is the... 

+ $\tau_i$ is the...

+ $p_m$ is the...

+ $\epsilon_{im}$ is the...

:::

:::{.version-solution}
for $i=$ 1, 2;	$m=$ 1, 2, .., 70

where:

+ $y_{im}$ is the *time taken to say the 100 words in $i^{th}$ test for the $m^{th}$ subject.*

+ $\mu$ is the *overall mean time taken to say the 100 words in this test.*

+ $\tau_i$ is the *effect of text color $i$ on the time taken to say the 100 words in this test.*

+ $p_m$ is the *random effect of the $m^{th} subject (block)*

+ $\epsilon_{im}$ is the *random error associated with the $i^{th}$ test for the $m^{th}$ subject.*

:::
